newsitem.title: USA: CBOT July wheat sets new 10-month high on HRW loss.
newsitem.headline: CBOT July wheat sets new 10-month high on HRW loss.

text.p: New crop July CBOT soft red winter wheat futures surged to a fresh 10-month high by midsession and nearly all contracts were in fast trading on escalating concerns about crop losses in U.S. hard red winter wheat and drought-related losses in EC wheat, especially France, traders said.

"There are all kinds of horror stories and they pulled some rain (forecast) out of Europe. All of a sudden we've gone from bearish to bullish in a week," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International.
The July contract jumped to a session high of $4.40 per bushel, a new 10-month high for that month.

On June 18 last year, July reached $4.40 per bushel and the contract high for that month of $4.65 was set on April 11, 1996. The recent high of $4.38 was set during the opening of futures trading Tuesday.

Traders cited persistent talk that the weekend freeze in the U.S. Great Plains may have damaged up to 200 million bushels of wheat. Early this week the market tumbled on reports a widely-followed analytical firm pegged the losses at only about 50 million bushels.
At 1115 CDT, wheat was one to seven cents higher, with May up 4-3/4 at $4.30 and July was up seven at $4.38.
Crop specialists Friday told Reuters that last week's freeze may have sliced more than 100 million bushels from the Kansas wheat crop and severe losses in Oklahoma also were likely.

"Those numbers for Kansas alone are not unrealistic," said Rollie Sears, a Kansas State University wheat breeder, of the 100 million bushel loss prospect. He toured the damaged areas this week. "The damage in the southern third of the state is worse than I thought," Sears said.
The market also took note of potential cold weather in the state again next week.

"We will have to keep our eye on next week," said Mike Palmerino, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp. in Lexington, Mass. "It looks like it will continue to cool off in the HRW (hard red winter wheat) belt."
Wheat values had surged Thursday on news the EU halted its weekly export tender program for wheat amid concerns about dry weather in Europe, especially France, a key wheat producer.
French weather forecasters Friday predicted another five days without rain across most of the country's farm districts.
Patrick Galois, forecaster with national weather service Meteo France, saw no rain on the horizon in northern France. That is a primary wheat, barley and sugar area.
